statement:
There are `n` piles of bananas, where pile `i` holds `piles[i]` bananas, and the guards return in `h` hours. Koko picks an eating speed of `k` bananas per hour. Each hour she chooses one pile and eats `k` bananas from it; if that pile has fewer than `k` left, she finishes it and waits out the rest of that hour without starting another pile.

solutions.name: Linear Search on Capacity
solutions.description: The capacity must be at least the heaviest package. Try capacities upward from there, simulating the greedy day-packing for each, and return the first one that fits within days.

code.bash:
shipWithinDays() {
    local -a weights
    read -ra weights <<< "$1"
    local days="$2" cap=0 w used load

    # days_needed cap -> used = days to ship everything with that capacity
    days_needed() {
        used=1; load=0
        for w in "${weights[@]}"; do
            if (( load + w > $1 )); then (( used++ )); load=0; fi
            (( load += w ))
        done
    }

    for w in "${weights[@]}"; do (( w > cap )) && cap=$w; done
    while days_needed "$cap"; (( used > days )); do (( cap++ )); done
    echo "$cap"
}

keyPoints: Greedy: fill a day until it overflows

solutions.name: Binary Search on Capacity + Greedy Check (Optimal)
solutions.description: Feasibility is monotone: if a capacity works, every larger one works. Binary search the smallest feasible capacity between max(weights) and sum(weights), checking each candidate with the greedy day count.

code.bash:
shipWithinDays() {
    local -a weights
    read -ra weights <<< "$1"
    local days="$2" lo=0 hi=0 w mid

    # fits cap: can everything ship within `days` at this capacity?
    fits() {
        local used=1 load=0
        for w in "${weights[@]}"; do
            if (( load + w > $1 )); then (( used++ )); load=0; fi
            (( load += w ))
        done
        (( used <= days ))
    }

    for w in "${weights[@]}"; do (( w > lo )) && lo=$w; (( hi += w )); done
    while (( lo < hi )); do
        mid=$(( (lo + hi) / 2 ))
        if fits "$mid"; then hi=$mid; else lo=$(( mid + 1 )); fi
    done
    echo "$lo"
}

keyPoints: lo = max weight, hi = total weight
Fits → hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1

solutions.name: Try Each Bloom Day in Order
solutions.description: The answer, if any, is one of the bloom days. Sort the distinct bloom days and test each with a linear scan counting runs of k adjacent bloomed flowers; the first day that yields m bouquets is the answer.

code.bash:
minDays() {
    local -a bloomDay days
    read -ra bloomDay <<< "$1"
    local m="$2" k="$3" day b made run
    if (( m * k > ${#bloomDay[@]} )); then echo -1; return; fi

    # bouquets day -> made = bouquets available on that day
    bouquets() {
        made=0; run=0
        for b in "${bloomDay[@]}"; do
            if (( b <= $1 )); then (( run++ )); else run=0; fi
            if (( run == k )); then (( made++ )); run=0; fi
        done
    }

    # distinct bloom days in ascending order
    mapfile -t days < <(printf '%s\n' "${bloomDay[@]}" | sort -n -u)
    for day in "${days[@]}"; do
        bouquets "$day"
        if (( made >= m )); then echo "$day"; return; fi
    done
    echo -1
}

keyPoints: Scan: count full runs of k

solutions.name: Binary Search on Day + Linear Scan (Optimal)
solutions.description: More days never reduce the bouquets you can make, so feasibility is monotone in the day. Binary search the smallest day in [min bloom, max bloom] for which a linear scan of adjacent runs yields at least m bouquets.

code.bash:
minDays() {
    local -a bloomDay
    read -ra bloomDay <<< "$1"
    local m="$2" k="$3" b lo hi mid
    if (( m * k > ${#bloomDay[@]} )); then echo -1; return; fi

    # can_make day: at least m bouquets of k adjacent bloomed flowers?
    can_make() {
        local made=0 run=0
        for b in "${bloomDay[@]}"; do
            if (( b <= $1 )); then (( run++ )); else run=0; fi
            if (( run == k )); then (( made++ )); run=0; fi
        done
        (( made >= m ))
    }

    lo=${bloomDay[0]}; hi=${bloomDay[0]}
    for b in "${bloomDay[@]}"; do (( b < lo )) && lo=$b; (( b > hi )) && hi=$b; done
    while (( lo < hi )); do
        mid=$(( (lo + hi) / 2 ))
        if can_make "$mid"; then hi=$mid; else lo=$(( mid + 1 )); fi
    done
    echo "$lo"
}

solutions.name: Linear Scan from Lower Bound
solutions.description: No speed below ceil(sum / h) can finish in time, so start there and try each speed upward until the total hours (sum of ceil(pile / speed)) fit within h.

code.bash:
minEatingSpeed() {
    local -a piles
    read -ra piles <<< "$1"
    local h="$2" sum=0 p speed hours
    for p in "${piles[@]}"; do (( sum += p )); done
    # no speed below ceil(sum / h) can finish in time
    speed=$(( (sum + h - 1) / h )); (( speed < 1 )) && speed=1
    while :; do
        hours=0
        for p in "${piles[@]}"; do (( hours += (p + speed - 1) / speed )); done
        if (( hours <= h )); then echo "$speed"; return; fi
        (( speed++ ))
    done
}

keyPoints: Hours at speed k = Σ ceil(p / k)
ceil(sum / h) is a hard lower bound
Still linear in the speed range

solutions.name: Binary Search on Speed (Optimal)
solutions.description: Feasibility is monotonic in speed, so binary search the smallest speed in [1, max(piles)] whose total hours fit within h.

code.bash:
minEatingSpeed() {
    local -a piles
    read -ra piles <<< "$1"
    local h="$2" lo=1 hi=0 p mid hours
    for p in "${piles[@]}"; do (( p > hi )) && hi=$p; done
    # smallest speed whose total hours fit in h
    while (( lo < hi )); do
        mid=$(( (lo + hi) / 2 ))
        hours=0
        for p in "${piles[@]}"; do (( hours += (p + mid - 1) / mid )); done
        if (( hours <= h )); then hi=$mid; else lo=$(( mid + 1 )); fi
    done
    echo "$lo"
}

keyPoints: Faster speed never needs more hours
